Paella is a famous Spanish rice dish. It comes from Valencia, a sunny region on the eastern coast of Spain, and it is considered one of Spain's most iconic and beloved foods. Today, it is enjoyed all over the world.

The word "paella" can refer to two closely related things: the dish itself (the food you eat) and the special cooking pan it is made in. In most everyday conversations, when someone says "paella," they almost always mean the food.

Paella is a large, flat, and colorful dish. It has a beautiful golden-yellow color, which comes from saffron — a spice made from the dried threads of a flower. Saffron is one of the most expensive spices in the world, and it is what gives paella its signature look and a subtle, earthy flavor.

The dish is typically cooked and served in a wide, round, shallow metal pan with two handles on the sides — and this pan is also called a "paella." The pan is wide and flat on purpose, because paella rice should spread out in a thin, even layer, not pile up like a mound. This allows the rice to cook properly and develop its most prized feature (more on that below).

Paella is a rice dish. The rice used is short-grain, which means each grain is small and slightly round. This type of rice absorbs liquid and flavor very well without turning mushy.

Beyond rice, paella contains a flavorful broth (sometimes made from meat, seafood, or vegetables), olive oil, garlic, tomatoes, and saffron. The other ingredients vary depending on the type of paella:

Paella Valenciana (the original and most traditional kind) contains chicken, rabbit, green beans, and large white butter beans. This is the "real" paella that people from Valencia will fiercely defend as the authentic version.

Seafood Paella is the type most people outside of Spain are familiar with. It contains ingredients like shrimp, mussels, clams, squid, and sometimes fish. No meat is added.

Mixed Paella combines both meat and seafood — a popular version in restaurants around the world, though traditionalists from Valencia may raise an eyebrow at it.

There are also regional and modern variations that use other proteins like duck, pork ribs, or vegetables only.
The Most Special Thing About Paella: The Socarrat

One of the most important and celebrated things about a well-made paella is something called the socarrat. This is the thin, crispy, slightly caramelized layer of rice that forms at the very bottom of the pan during the final moments of cooking.

A good socarrat is not burnt — it is toasted, nutty, and crunchy. It is considered a sign that the cook has done their job well. People who love paella will often scrape the bottom of the pan specifically to get to this layer. If a paella does not have a socarrat, many consider it incomplete.

Paella is cooked over heat — traditionally over an open wood fire outdoors, which adds a smoky depth of flavor. Today, many people cook it on a gas stove or a special outdoor burner.

The cooking process is done entirely in the pan itself, in stages. First, the meat or seafood is browned in olive oil. Then, vegetables and tomatoes are cooked down. Broth and saffron are added next, and when the liquid is boiling, the rice is spread out evenly across the pan. From that point on, the rice is never stirred. This is crucial. Stirring would make it starchy and sticky, more like risotto. Paella rice must stay separate and loose, each grain soaking up flavor on its own.

Paella is a deeply communal, social dish. In Spain — especially in Valencia — it is a tradition to gather family and friends on Sundays, cook a large paella outdoors, and eat it straight from the pan, each person eating from their own section. It is a meal that brings people together.

In restaurants, it is sometimes served in individual portions, but many places still serve it in the pan at the table for a group to share.

Because paella is famous worldwide, it is often misrepresented. Here are some important clarifications:

  • It is not a quick or casual dish. Making a proper paella takes care, the right ingredients, and attention. A rushed or poorly made paella will not have the right texture or flavor.
  • It should not be mushy or sticky. If the rice is soft and clumped together, that is a sign it was overcooked or stirred too much.
  • It is not the same as Spanish rice or fried rice. Those are entirely different dishes with different methods, textures, and flavors.
  • Adding chorizo is controversial. Many Spaniards, especially those from Valencia, consider adding chorizo (a spiced sausage) to paella a serious mistake and an insult to the dish's tradition — even though you will find it in many international restaurants.

Paella is a wide, flat, saffron-golden rice dish from Valencia, Spain. It is cooked in a special shallow pan of the same name, without stirring, to achieve a crispy rice crust at the bottom called the socarrat. It comes in several varieties — most notably the traditional Valencian version with chicken and rabbit, and the internationally popular seafood version. It is more than just food; it is a cultural ritual of gathering, sharing, and taking pride in something made with care.
